title: Triangulations
notes: Open with the chapter question: when is a topological problem allowed to become a finite incidence problem? The dependency map is not a syllabus decoration; it shows that subdivision, carriers, edge loops, quotient triangulations, and local finiteness are mutually supporting proof tools.

title: Simplicial Complexes
notes: Spend time on the intersection condition. A drawing can look triangular and still fail to be a simplicial complex if overlaps create extra crossing data. The usable object is the incidence rule plus compatible geometry, so every intersection is already a face of both simplexes.

title: Incidence Ledger
notes: This slide turns the definition into checkable data. The f-vector is not yet topology, because subdivision will change it, but the alternating sum and boundary maps are stable signals. Point out that the torus row already anticipates quotient models later in the lecture.

title: Barycentric Subdivision
notes: Emphasize the chain rule for new simplexes: vertex less than edge less than face. The count increase is deliberate, not noise. The mesh shrinks while the underlying polyhedron and Euler characteristic stay fixed, which is exactly why subdivision is a proof machine.

title: Mesh Shrink Roadmap
notes: The proof idea is an open-cover argument written in combinatorial language. Pull target stars back along the continuous map, subdivide until domain stars are small enough, and then make vertex choices. This is where local geometry buys finite combinatorics.

title: Simplicial Approximation
notes: Use the x squared example as a carrier test, not as the theorem itself. The coarse middle vertex cannot be assigned compatibly, while the refined domain has enough local choices. The homotopy is protected because original and chosen images lie in common simplexes.

title: Triangulation Restrictions
notes: This is the caution slide. Triangulation is stronger than drawing triangles on a space. The face-closure condition, common-face intersections, quotient compatibility, and local finiteness are all restrictions that prevent a picture from lying about the topology.

title: Edge Paths
notes: Connect this back to the previous chapter without re-proving it. The edge group is a finite model for fundamental-group calculations: choose a maximal tree, keep the non-tree edges as generators, and let filled triangles impose local shortcut relations.

title: Edge Group Ledger
notes: Read the table as a calculation recipe. The bouquet has no triangle relations, so two non-tree edges generate a free group. The quotient-surface words show how the same edge-path method records the familiar torus, Klein bottle, and projective-plane presentations.

title: Quotient Surface Models
notes: A fundamental polygon is a compact symbolic description of edge identifications. It is not automatically a simplicial complex, but it tells a compatible triangulation what must match along the boundary. The Euler characteristic here comes from the quotient cell ledger.

title: Torus Mesh Check
notes: The embedded torus is a sanity check for the quotient model. It should not be mistaken for the definition of the torus. The important facts are watertightness, the Euler count, and the Betti pattern, all of which survive the particular geometric embedding.

title: Refinement Lab
notes: The lab is a falsifiability check. As the periodic grid is refined, the number of vertices, edges, and triangles grows quickly, while chi and the Betti numbers stay fixed. The decreasing edge length shows why refinement improves geometry without changing topology.

title: Orbit Triangulations
notes: Explain the vertex scheme slowly: the quotient remembers vertex orbits and which orbit sets came from original simplexes. The second barycentric subdivision is a technical but useful repair, because it prevents bad identifications inside a small simplex from corrupting the quotient complex.

title: Local Finiteness
notes: This is where infinite examples become respectable. Local finiteness keeps neighborhoods from meeting infinitely many unrelated simplexes, so the gluing topology behaves like the Euclidean subspace topology. The accumulation panel shows why this condition is not cosmetic.

title: Proof Roadmaps
notes: Use the dependency map as a proof navigation tool. Subdivision supplies small stars, approximation turns maps into vertex data, edge groups turn loops into presentations, and orbit triangulations make quotient spaces combinatorial after enough controlled refinement.

title: What Changes
notes: This comparison is the central habit of the chapter. Triangulations are adjustable models, so counts and mesh sizes can change. The polyhedron, Euler characteristic, homotopy information, quotient type, and local finiteness checks are the data that should remain meaningful.

title: Recap
notes: Close by asking students to identify which proof move they are seeing in any triangulation argument. Is the author refining, choosing carriers, calculating an edge group, enforcing quotient compatibility, or checking local finiteness? That diagnostic question is the chapter's transferable skill.
